The obelisk in this square dates from 1814, which marks São Paulo becoming a city.
The square holds São Bento's church and monastery, a 17th century monastery, where mass is still held against a backdrop of Gregorian chants. The monks' bakery is a temptation. Give in, it’s no sin.
Church and Convent of Saint Francis and the historic Law School of the University of São Paulo.

São Paulo's central square (marked by the Zero Mark (Marco Zero) monument) has fountains, 16 sculptures, palm trees and lots and lots of people. The Sé Cathedral and the São Paulo Justice Palace are located here.
The valley is a giant boulevard with gardens, sculptures and a view of the main downtown office buildings. The Altino Arantes building and the Correios Palace are here.
Linking R. Barão de Itapetininga to R. Direita. Marks the transition from old to the new part of the center.
This exchange is the largest in South America, founded in 1890 by Emílio Rangel Pestana. You can have a visit to the museum inside the building, showcasing Brazil's economic history.

Previously known as the Banespa building (after the bank that used to occupy the building), it was the tallest skyscraper in the city between its completion in 1947 and the construction of the Itália building in 1965. Aside from art…

São Paulo's city hall is a building from the 1930s in modernist architectural style. The building had been the home of Matarazzo Industries, which used to be the most powerful manufacturing company in Brazil.
The first home to the state's mail service, constructed in 1922. It hosts many exhibitions, mainly focused on the company's history.
Home to the Higher Courts of Law of the State of São Paulo since 1933. Hosts an exhibition about law in the state.
Emperor Dom Pedro I's powerful concubine, the Marchess of Santos is one of the most popular monarchy figures in Brazilian popular culture. Her colonial house is now a museum.

A creepy-looking church in a small street near Liberdade Sq., it is one of the oldest surviving churches of the city, dating back to 1774, when it was built to be the chapel of the city's first cemetery. It is still the destination of…

São Paulo's main catholic church, with 14 towers, built in a Gothic and Renaissance style. Although the current construction was finished in 1954, the original cathedral, at the same spot, dates from the early history of São Paulo - 1616.
Our Lady of Good Death Church

Known in the past as “Igreja das Boas Notícias” (Church of Good News) due to its bells tolling whenever someone important arrived in São Paulo, the historical church opened in 1810. Local legend says its curious name is due to the fact…
A church from the colonial period, finished in 1758, with the original building dating back to 1592. Contains over a hundred pieces of art from the colonial area.

Built in a neo-romantic style with neo-gothic details, it resembles medieval churches in northern Europe. It was temporarily the cathedral of São Paulo between 1930 and 1954. Contains paintings of Henri Bernard, Benedito Calixto and…
Former São Paulo city hall, constructed during the 1920s in an eclectic style. It now hosts an interactive science museum, a very popular choice to take the kids to.

Dedicated to one of the city's founders, José de Anchieta, and also the place where São Paulo was founded on January 25, 1554. It contains many paintings and historic documents, the most interesting of which is a scale model of early…

Opened in 1929, this building's purpose changed along with its leadership, going from a movie theater to a live performance theater. Hosts the most popular Broadway-style musicals south of the equator, translated into Portuguese.

One of the two traditional addresses for classical music fans. This is where the historic Modern Art Week took place in 1922. The building, designed by Ramos de Azevedo in 1911, is reason enough to justify a visit. It now houses the São…
Once the bank’s first headquarters in São Paulo — offers an excellent program of arts, movies, theater and music at accessible prices.

The historical part of downtown is known for being unsafe at night, so to compensate for that, local NGOs organize a nocturnal walking tour every Thursday. It is an opportunity to have a different look at some of downtown's most famous…

At this weekend open market, you can taste Asian delicacies like gyoza, takoyaki and okonomiyaki as well as non-Asian treats like acarajé from Bahia. Look for unusual sweets like ginger ice cream or even tempura-fried ice-cream.

A truly traditional outing in São Paulo, the "Big Market" is a mosaic of color and flavor that showcases a little something from all the different nationalities that settled in the capital. Pop in to sample the most beloved pastries and…

Typical Japanese ramen shop, where you are greeted with an irasshai-mase (welcome in Japanese) at the door and noodle-slurping noises from the Japanese customers. Also has great gyozas as side dishes.
Traditional Brazilian food with minor Japanese touches. Also serves yakisoba.

A Chinese restaurant famous for authentic and tasty Cantonese dishes with cheap and generous portions. Communicating with the staff can be a challenge, as many only speak Chinese, but the food is worth the while. Reservations only for…
Japanese restaurant with an extensive menu. Try the fried oysters or the yosenabe, stewed white fish with vegetables.
A mix of restaurant, karaoke and snooker bar, this unimaginable place packs on Thursdays and Fridays and is often featured on TV. Get in after 22:00.
